To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
melt inclusions, or magma samples ‘frozen’ within olivine phenocryts, show that the Hawaiian mantle sources are not concentrically zonned.

1) melt inclusions from the Hawaiian shield stage record the presence of two distinct source components, 2) these source components are not zoned concentrically around a central hot spot, 3) the source components are present in all shield-stage lavas regardless of their geographic location, and 4) the source components may be controlled by the thermal (rather than chemical) structure of the plumes.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the chemical structure of the mantle plume beneath Hawaii, which is the source of the Hawaiian–Emperor chain of volcanic islands.
the chemical structure of a mantle plume and the implications this has for the formation of ocean islands.
the chemical structure of mantle plumes, and the processes that lead to their formation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Hawaiian plume is a complex, non-zoned, thermally structured plume.
the chemical structure of the mantle plume beneath the Hawaiian islands is not concentrically zonal.
the Hawaiian–Emperor hotspot track is the result of an anomalously hot mantle plume that is not concentrically zonally, but is rather laterally zonally (i.e. azimuthally) zoned.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chemical structure of the Hawaii mantle plume is not as simple and straightforward as we previously thought.

the Hawaiian mantle is chemically heterogeneous, and that the observed chemical variation in the Hawaiian volcanoes is likely to be controlled by a combination of the thermal structure of a single, large mantle source and the thermal and chemical structure of the overlying lithosphere.

the Hawaiian mantle source is a complex, chemically heterogeneous mixture, which is likely to be the case for most mantle plumes, and that the observed compositional differences are not a function of plume geometry.
The main takeaway from our work is that
melt inclusions provide a new and important tool for understanding the chemical structure of mantle plumes.
the mantle plume source region is likely to be more complex and variable than is generally thought, and that melt inclusions may be an important tool to unravel its structure.
the Hawaiian plume is a chemically and thermally complex structure, and that it is not well represented by the traditional ‘hotspot’ model.
